June 25, 2026 — 11 papers analyzed
KEY FINDINGS
NYC's deployed congestion-pricing program shows transit ridership gains that
extend beyond the priced Manhattan core, even as overall demand falls there.
A fare-free bus simulation finds outsized equity benefits for lower-income NYC
riders, with only modest revenue trade-offs versus distance-based pricing.
A risk-aware planner remediates a median 53.6% of transit-desert tracts across
25 cities, beating static demographic scoring by 5 points on average.
PAPER OF THE DAY
Public transit gains and spatially uneven travel demand
changes after NYC congestion pricing
Donghang Li, Dingyi Zhuang, Yunlin Li, Chenan Shen, Nina Cao, Yunhan Zheng, Shenhao Wang, Jinhua Zhao
Using time-series foundation models to build calibrated counterfactual demand forecasts, the study
finds New York's cordon congestion-pricing program produced real bus and subway ridership gains that
extend well beyond the priced zone itself, while overall travel demand fell mainly inside it.
Congestion pricing has been argued almost entirely from pre-deployment models; this is one of the
first papers to evaluate the actual, live NYC program with a methodologically serious

Transit agencies weighing fare reform should treat fare-free bus programs as the highest-

Agencies planning transit-desert investment should adopt belief-updating, risk-aware
sequencing instead of static demographic scoring, particularly at moderate budget levels
